---
title: Lazy Operations
---

A patch whose data are not read yet holds a [`LazyArray`](`dascore.lazy.array.LazyArray`): a [`Recipe`](`dascore.lazy.recipe.Recipe`), which says which stored samples fill which box of the array, and a chain of the operations run on it since. An operation on such a patch computes nothing. Its kernel appends the processor and its plan to the chain, and [`Patch.load`](`dascore.Patch.load`) runs the chain: on the whole array when that is small, and a chunk at a time when it is not. The rules below are what let the work be split without changing any result. The code cells execute against the real machinery, so this note fails the doc build if it drifts from the implementation.

```{python}
import numpy as np

import dascore as dc
from dascore.core.source import ArraySource
from dascore.lazy.recipe import Recipe

recipe = Recipe.from_source(ArraySource.full((4, 3), -2.0))
coords = {"distance": np.arange(4), "time": np.arange(3)}
lazy = dc.Patch(data=recipe, coords=coords, dims=("distance", "time"))

out = lazy.abs().update_attrs(station="here").angle()
print(out.backend, len(out.data.chain))
```

## The rules a lazy operation keeps

**Chunk size is an implementation detail.** The result is the same, within floating-point precision, whether it was computed whole or a chunk at a time, and it has the same `data_id`. An operation states what a chunk of its output needs of its input by returning a [chunk contract](`dascore.lazy.contract`) from [`chunk_contract`](`dascore.core.processor.PatchProcessor.chunk_contract`), given the input's dtype and its plan. The contracts are listed [below](#the-contracts). A contract is decided from the dtype and the plan, never from the values: an operation whose no-op depends on the values, such as `fillna`, cannot state one.

**Metadata is never lazy.** A lazy patch always has concrete coords, attrs, shape and dtype. They come from `get_metadata`, which runs when the operation is called and knows nothing of chunks, so it must state the dtype the kernel returns as well as the shape. [`load`](`dascore.lazy.array.LazyArray.load`) checks each step's result against what its metadata stated, and refuses a mismatch naming the processor. An operation whose metadata depends on the data cannot be lazy.

```{python}
loaded = out.load()
assert loaded.dtype == out.dtype and loaded.shape == out.shape
```

**The lazy backend never falls back.** An operation with no contract raises [`LazyOperationError`](`dascore.exceptions.LazyOperationError`) before anything is read, where another backend would convert to NumPy. So do arithmetic and NumPy functions on the patch, whichever operand is lazy, and `rolling`, stacking a spool, and the waterfall and specplot figures. A patch's repr describes lazy data without reading them. The data are read in these places only:

- `Patch.load` (and `Spool.load`, which calls it), `np.asarray(patch)`, and writing the patch to a file, where the caller asks for the values;
- `Patch.equals` (and `==`), which compares them;
- taking a merged patch from a spool, as `spool.chunk(time=None)[0]` does, since that is how a spool loads; a merge which stays lazy is a later feature.

Everything else refuses.

```{python}
from dascore.exceptions import LazyOperationError

try:
    lazy.detrend("time")
except LazyOperationError as error:
    print(error)
```

**Each step has its own identity.** A step's `data_id` is the one [`PatchProcessor`](`dascore.core.processor.PatchProcessor`) records for an eager patch: derived from the operation's id and the previous patch's `data_id`. The node records the id the patch was given at that step, so every lazy step has the eager step's id, and an eager no-op (an `Unchanged` contract) hands back the patch itself, id and all. A metadata-only operation changes the patch's id and leaves the lazy array as it was; the patch's `attrs.data_id` is what names the patch.

```{python}
eager = lazy.load().abs().update_attrs(station="here").angle()
assert loaded.attrs.data_id == eager.attrs.data_id == out.attrs.data_id
assert lazy.real() is lazy  # real data: nothing to do, as eagerly
```

## The contracts

A chunk is a box of the array: one slice for each axis. A contract says which box of its input a box of its output is computed from, and nothing else about chunks; no operation chooses a chunk size or loops over chunks.

| Contract | A box of the output needs | Stated by |
|---|---|---|
| `Pointwise` | the same box of the input | `abs`, `real`, `imag`, `angle`, `conj` |
| `Halo` | the same box and a fixed number of samples around it, stopping at the ends of the array | `median_filter`, `gaussian_filter`, and `savgol_filter` with an edge mode other than its default |
| `WholeAxis` | the whole of some axes, and the same place along the others | `pass_filter`; the three above when their edge mode wraps; `savgol_filter` in its default mode, which fits a polynomial to each end of what it is given |
| `Window` | the same box moved by where a selection starts | `select` with ranges |
| `Tiles` | the tiles which overlap the box, each whole; along the other axes, what the operation in the window states | a patch operation called on a [`Patch.window`](`dascore.Patch.window`) |
| `Unchanged` | nothing: the kernel hands its input back | `real` and `conj` of real data, a `select` which keeps everything |

The filters state a contract for `float32` and `float64` data only, the dtypes their kernels return as given, and `gaussian_filter` states none when its edge mode is given axis by axis. A query which does not resolve to one range for each dimension is no window and is refused: a `select` by an array of values or a mask, and what `unselect` and `order` build.

A patch operation called on a window is computed a tile at a time and blended, so it states `Tiles` whatever the operation is. The tiles are placed by the array and not by the box: a box is grown out to the edges of the tiles which overlap it, each of those is computed whole, and the box is cut from the blend. A windowed axis can therefore be cut even where the operation alone needs it whole, and `window(time=10).detrend("time")` runs on a lazy patch where `detrend("time")` is refused. Along an axis which is not windowed the box needs what the operation's own contract says, and the whole axis where it states none. Where the operation keeps every n-th sample of a windowed axis, as `fbe` with a `step` does, the result is shorter than what it is computed from: a box is of the result, the tiles which overlap it are found in the samples the operation makes, and what is read is those tiles of the input. The lazy patch states its dtype by running the operation's kernel once on a window of zeros, since an operation with no contract has never had to state what its kernel returns. A reduction in a window and a function given to `apply` state no contract yet, so both are refused on a lazy patch.

A `Halo` kernel sees the true ends of the array in the chunks which hold them, so it treats them as it does eagerly, and what it makes of a cut end is trimmed off. A halo never reaches past an earlier selection: to a filter after a `select`, the window's ends are the array's.

## How a chain runs

[`dascore.lazy.execute`](`dascore.lazy.execute`) does the work in three separate steps.

1. **Cut the result into boxes.** If no array the result needs is larger than the `lazy_block_size` setting, there is one box. There is also one box when no step computes anything, since reading in pieces would only open each file again. Otherwise the box is halved along the first axis worth cutting until they fit. An axis an operation needs whole is not worth cutting, and nor is one already short beside its halo, so the block size is aimed for rather than promised.
2. **Work out what each box reads.** Each step's contract is asked, last to first, which box of its input it needs. Nothing is read to answer, so every read is known before the first one happens.
3. **Read and compute each box.** The recipe reads only the box needed, and each step's NumPy kernel runs on it, first to last.

A selection therefore narrows what is read wherever it sits in the chain.

```{python}
from dascore.lazy.execute import chunk_boxes, read_schedule

recipe = Recipe.from_source(ArraySource.full((8, 1_000), 1.0))
coords = {"distance": np.arange(8), "time": np.arange(1_000)}
big = dc.Patch(data=recipe, coords=coords, dims=("distance", "time"))

chain = big.median_filter(time=5, samples=True).select(time=(100, 200), samples=True)
boxes = chunk_boxes(chain.data)
print(boxes, read_schedule(chain.data, boxes))
```

The whole result is still put together in memory; writing each box out as it is made is a later change, and [Windowed and Lazy Processing](windowed_processing.qmd) is the plan for it and for what else is to come. Until then:

- Nothing is kept between loads. Each piece a spool cuts from a lazy patch runs the chain for itself, so a piece cut along an axis a step needs whole reads and computes that whole axis again.
- A kernel is not run until the chain is, so an argument its kernel refuses, such as an edge mode scipy does not know, is refused at `load` rather than at the call.
- A step which recorded no contract, as a kernel registered for the lazy backend may leave, is given all of its input.

## Where it happens

[`kernel_for`](`dascore.core.processor.PatchProcessor.kernel_for`) answers the lazy backend with a class's own registered lazy kernel, or else with [`lazy_kernel`](`dascore.lazy.kernels.lazy_kernel`), for the first class in the MRO which computes, whether by a kernel it writes or one registered on it; a class with none stays metadata-only. The generic kernel asks for the contract only when it describes the kernel which runs -- the class stating it is the class owning that kernel, or a subclass of it -- and refuses an operation which overrides `reconcile`, which would be handed the lazy array. For any contract but `Unchanged` it then appends a pending node, recording the contract on it. `PatchProcessor` settles that node with the output shape, dtype and `data_id` once the result's attrs are final and before the patch is built.

## Why not dask

Dask plans its work as a graph holding a task for every chunk of every operation. For very large arrays, building and scheduling that graph costs more than the work it describes. A chain holds one node for each operation, whatever the size of the array, and how the work is split into boxes is decided only when it runs.

A dask array is still accepted as a patch's data, as any other array backend is, and its dispatch is unchanged: an operation runs on dask where its kernel can, and otherwise falls back to NumPy with a warning; a patch operation run in the windows of a [`Patch.window`](`dascore.Patch.window`) is the exception, computed a piece at a time from the windows which overlap each piece; a reduction there still falls back, and `apply` gives back NumPy data. None of the rules above hold for it. `Patch.load` reads a dask-backed patch into memory as well, and [`Spool.io.to_xarray`](`dascore.xarray.spool.spool_to_xarray`) builds dask arrays because that is how xarray defers a read. For data larger than memory within DASCore, the lazy backend is the one to use.
